sentences.text: The holotype — the single specimen used to define the species — preserves an articulated right hindlimb containing the thigh bone, shin bones, and foot.
Measurements show the longest shin bone reached 270 mm, while the longest thigh bone measured 247 mm.
Because the shin bone averaged 13% longer than the thigh bone, the animal likely adapted for running.

Distinctive anatomical features include deep grooves on the neck vertebrae, a broad opening in the spine canal, ridges on the tail bones, strong hand claws, narrow foot bones, and a deep notch on the thigh bone.
Estimates place the total body length between 2 and 3 meters and the weight between 35 and 45 kg.
Bone tissue analysis indicates that the known individuals were juveniles or sub-adults, with some reaching approximately three years of age.
Fossils were unearthed in 1995 at the Laguna Rancho Palacios site within the Chubut province of Argentina.
The name translates to 'spring lizard' because the find occurred on September 21, the date spring begins in the Southern Hemisphere.
Although the name was coined in 1997, Rubén Dario Martínez and Fernando Emilio Novas formally described the species Aniksosaurus darwini in 2006.
The specific name darwini honors Charles Darwin, who explored Patagonia during his travels in 1832 and 1833.
Four additional individuals, designated as paratypes, were also discovered at this same location.
Fossil beds containing only this species suggest the animals lived in groups, which may have offered protection against rivals.
This social behavior likely occurred only during a specific life stage, probably when the animals were sub-adults.
Small scavengers probably consumed parts of the carcass, leaving tiny grooves on the thigh bones after soft tissues decomposed.
Researchers found no signs that individuals ate each other or fought over resources within the group.
Martínez and Novas originally placed the genus in the clade Coelurosauria based on the structure of the hind limbs.
Later studies by Choiniere and colleagues in 2010 showed the animal is more closely related to the family Compsognathidae.
Consequently, the parent group for this taxon is now identified as Compsognathidae.
The animal lived during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages of the Cretaceous period, roughly 96 to 91 million years ago.
Radiometric dating confirms the fossils were deposited between 96 and 91 million years ago, though some ranges extend to 100.5 and 89.8 million years ago.
The environment also held remains of Xenotarsosaurus, Drusilasaura, Epachthosaurus, Campylodoniscus, Secernosaurus, and teeth from large predators like carcharodontosaurids and dromaeosaurids.
